title: API Design Best Practices
description: Learn best practices for designing robust and maintainable APIs between microservices.

data.text: Well-designed APIs are the backbone of maintainable microservices. Google, Amazon, and Netflix all enforce strict API design guidelines because poor APIs create cascading integration problems across hundreds of services.

data.title: Essential Principles
items: Use nouns, not verbs, for resource paths: /users, not /getUsers
Use plural nouns for collections: /users/123/orders, not /user/123/order
Use standard HTTP status codes correctly
Provide consistent error responses with machine-readable codes

data.title: Versioning Approaches
items: Content negotiation: Accept: application/vnd.example.v1+json (RESTful but complex)
GraphQL: No versioning needed; evolve schema with deprecation

data.title: Backward Compatibility
data.text: Always design for backward compatibility. Add new fields; never remove or rename existing ones without a version bump. Netflix maintains API compatibility for months to give consumers time to migrate.

data.title: Example: Good vs Bad API Design
data.code:
# Bad API design
GET /getUser?id=123
POST /createOrder
GET /getOrdersForUser?userId=123

# Good API design
GET /v1/users/123
POST /v1/orders
GET /v1/users/123/orders

# Consistent error format
{
  "error": {
    "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
    "message": "Email is required",
    "field": "email"
  }
}

data.caption: API lifecycle and versioning
data.definition:
graph LR
    A[Design API] --> B[Publish Contract]
    B --> C[Implement Service]
    C --> D[Version When Breaking]
    D --> E[Deprecate Old Version]
    E --> F[Remove After Grace Period]
    F --> A

items.question: How often should I version APIs?
items.answer: Only when you make breaking changes. Additive changes (new fields, new endpoints) do not require versioning if they are backward compatible.

items.question: What is OpenAPI?
items.answer: OpenAPI (formerly Swagger) is a specification for describing REST APIs. It enables code generation, documentation, and testing. Use it for contract-first API design.

items.question: Should I use API contracts?
items.answer: Yes. Contract-first design catches breaking changes before they reach production. Tools like OpenAPI and gRPC proto files serve as contracts.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Design APIs for consumers, not just implementers
Version APIs only when making breaking changes
Use contracts to define and validate APIs
data.takeaway: Good API design reduces integration bugs and makes microservices easier to evolve independently.
